name: Media
blurb: Generation tools transformed production while training-data litigation transformed the business relationship with AI; cross-linked to the lawsuit tracker.

points.desc: The US Copyright Office AI policy programme, covering registrability of AI-assisted works, training on copyrighted material, and digital replicas, is the primary legal reference for anyone publishing AI-assisted media in the United States.
points.name: The Copyright Office is writing the rules

points.desc: Article 50 of the EU AI Act sets transparency obligations for AI-generated and manipulated content, including deepfakes. It applies to publishers distributing into the EU regardless of where the content was made.
points.name: Synthetic media carries a disclosure duty in the EU

points.desc: C2PA publishes the open technical specification for content credentials: cryptographically signed provenance that travels with an image, video, or audio file. It is the standards-body answer to the question of what a newsroom attaches to a synthetic asset.
points.name: Provenance is being standardised, not invented per outlet

points.desc: The Associated Press documents its own AI use in production, including transcription, shotlisting, and metadata. It is an operating newsroom describing deployed systems rather than a vendor describing a roadmap.
points.name: A wire service publishing what it actually does

points.desc: AP publishes its standards for generative AI in journalism, covering what may be produced with it, what must be verified, and what may not be published. One of the few newsroom policies available to read in full rather than summarised.
points.name: Newsroom rules written down and published

points.desc: The Reuters Institute Digital News Report at Oxford surveys news consumption across dozens of markets, including audience trust in AI-assisted journalism and newsroom adoption. Survey-based and published in full.
points.name: Audience data on AI in news, measured annually

points.desc: The Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia publishes research on algorithmic distribution, newsroom tools, and the business ethics of AI in media, independent of the vendors selling the tools.
points.name: Independent research on newsroom AI tooling

points.desc: The Stanford HAI AI Index tracks technical progress, investment, and adoption annually, with data points covering creative media and journalism. Useful for placing a media-specific claim against the wider trend.
points.name: The field-wide numbers, including creative work

summary: Generation tools transformed production while training-data litigation transformed the business relationship with AI.

analysis.body:
According to the Census Bureau, 43.5 percent of firms in the Information sector (NAICS 51, which includes media) reported using AI in the preceding two weeks as of the latest survey, down from 46.0 percent in the prior period. This adoption baseline masks significant variation in how media organizations deploy AI and the constraints they face in doing so.

The Associated Press illustrates the production layer where AI has embedded itself. AP uses AI-driven tools to analyze video content and generate shotlists, to conduct AI-powered search that recognizes visual elements without relying on descriptions, and to analyze federal registry data to surface local news tips in collaboration with AppliedXL. All generated descriptions are reviewed by editorial staff before publication. AP has also developed five AI projects as part of a Local News AI initiative funded by the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation. This toolkit does not replace journalists; according to AP's published standards, the central role of the journalist in gathering, evaluating and ordering facts remains unchanged, and any output from a generative AI tool must be treated as unvetted source material subject to AP's sourcing standards.

The regulatory posture has shifted sharply toward disclosure and provenance. In the European Union, Article 50 of the AI Act requires that providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, with technical solutions required to be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible. Deployers generating or manipulating image, audio or video content constituting a deepfake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The U.S. Copyright Office has launched a multi-part study since early 2023 examining copyright issues raised by AI, including the scope of copyright in AI-generated works and the use of copyrighted materials in AI training, publishing Part 1 on digital replicas on July 31, 2024, and Part 2 on the copyrightability of outputs created using generative AI on January 29, 2025. Newsroom standards are emerging independently; AP's published guidance specifies that the organization does not alter any elements of photos, video or audio and will not transmit any AI-generated images that are suspected or proven to be false depictions of reality, though AI-generated illustrations may be used if clearly labeled as such in captions.

Technical standards for content provenance are being built outside individual newsrooms. The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity publishes Content Credentials, an open technical standard that functions as a nutrition label for digital content, allowing publishers, creators and consumers to establish the origin and edits of digital content. This standard provides a way to ensure content transparency by analyzing the origin of media, with credentials readable by anyone at any time. The standard sits between regulatory mandate and operational practice, enabling the machine-readable marking required by the EU AI Act and providing the infrastructure newsrooms need to track synthetic assets through distribution.

Litigation has become endemic. Live tracking shows 103 major AI lawsuits involving copyright, privacy and safety cases against AI companies, with copyright cases naming entities including Perplexity AI, X.AI, Stability AI, and Runway AI. These cases directly affect media training data pipelines and the legal risk of republishing AI-assisted work. Organizations deciding whether to deploy AI in media should expect that regulatory compliance—particularly disclosure of synthetic content and maintenance of content provenance—will be mandatory in major markets within the survey period, that editorial review of all AI outputs remains non-negotiable, and that the copyright status of both training data and generated outputs remains unsettled law subject to ongoing congressional action.

https://c2pa.org/.brief: The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) offers an open technical standard that lets publishers, creators and consumers verify the origin and edits of digital media. C2PA reports that its Content Credentials system provides a transparent record of a piece’s history, described as a “nutrition label” for digital content. According to C2PA, the credentials help ensure compliance with evolving standards and enhance digital safety. The organization says the system benefits publishers, creators, news media and policymakers by promoting transparency in their work.

https://www.copyright.gov/ai/.brief: The U.S. Copyright Office launched an AI initiative in early 2023 to examine how copyright law applies to AI-generated works and to the use of copyrighted material in AI training. After holding public listening sessions and webinars, it issued a notice of inquiry in the Federal Register in August 2023, gathering more than 10,000 comments by December 2023. The Office is publishing a multi-part report on AI: Part 1, released July 31 2024, covers digital replicas; Part 2, released January 29 2025, examines the copyrightability of generative-AI outputs. A pre-publication of Part 3 was released May 9 2025 in response to congressional questions and stakeholder interest, with a final version expected later but unlikely to change the analysis or conclusions.

https://www.cjr.org/tow_center.brief: The Tow Center for Digital Journalism, part of Columbia’s Graduate School of Journalism, studies how technology is reshaping journalism. It examines changes in how journalism is practiced and how audiences consume news. The center also looks for new methods to assess the reliability, standards, and credibility of online information. Its research aims to help the field adapt to evolving digital media landscapes.

https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/art.brief: According to the EU AI Act, providers must design AI systems that interact directly with people so that users are informed they are dealing with AI, unless it is obvious to a reasonably well-informed person. The Act also requires that providers of systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text mark the outputs in a machine-readable format and make them detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Deployers of AI systems that create deep-fake content must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The Commission will promote codes of practice to support detection, marking and labelling of such content, while the provisions do not override other transparency obligations under EU or national law.

https://www.ap.org/solutions/artificial-.brief: AP uses AI to streamline news production, employing AI-driven tools that analyze video content and generate shotlists that editors review before publishing. It partners with AppliedXL to analyze federal registry data for actionable news tips, collaborates with ShortTok for AI-powered content discovery, and uses Merlin AI search to recognize elements in photos and videos without relying on metadata. In 2023, AP launched five AI projects funded by the Knight Foundation, and its 2024 report “Generative AI in Journalism: The Evolution of Newswork and Ethics in a Generative Information Ecosystem” shows how news organizations worldwide are adopting AI tools while addressing ethical concerns and the need for human oversight. AP also offers a grant-funded training program and a new AI chapter in its Stylebook, and its 2022 report titled *“Artificial Intelligence in Local News: A survey of US newsrooms’ AI readiness”* examined challenges for smaller outlets, winning national awards and prompting government action.

https://www.copyright.gov/policy/artific.brief: The U.S. Copyright Office is conducting a study on copyright issues raised by artificial intelligence, gathering information and policy views to analyze the current law, spot unresolved problems, and assess possible congressional action. The Office released Part 1 on July 31, 2024, covering “digital replicas,” and Part 2 on January 29, 2025, focusing on the copyrightability of generative-AI outputs. A pre-publication of Part 3 appeared on May 9, 2025, in response to congressional inquiries and stakeholder interest. The Office expects the final Part 3 to be published later with no substantive changes to its analysis or conclusions.

https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac..brief: The page lists a podcast series that covers the Digital News Report 2026’s key findings, news creators, why traditional news organisations are losing audiences, AI and the future of news, the rise of news video, attitudes toward impartiality, and the social benefits of public-service news. It also offers a search interface with topics ranging from AI and journalism to audience engagement, business of news, climate journalism, conflict reporting, COVID-19, data journalism, foreign correspondence, investigative journalism, Israel-Gaza war, journalism and elections, journalism beats, journalism in exile, journalists at work, local news, media regulation, mental health, misinformation, news avoidance, news creators, news podcasts, newsroom diversity, newsroom leadership, OSINT platforms and social media, polarisation, press freedom, public-service media, solutions journalism, trust in news, war in Ukraine, and workplace conditions. The page serves as a hub for exploring the 2026 Digital News Report’s content. It is part of the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism’s annual audience-data research.

https://www.ap.org/the-definitive-source.brief: AP says accuracy, fairness, and speed guide its reporting, and it believes that careful use of generative AI can support those values and improve workflow. The organization stresses that journalists remain central to gathering, evaluating, and ordering facts, and AI is not seen as a replacement. AP’s guidance treats any output from a generative AI tool as “unvetted source material,” requiring editorial judgment and adherence to sourcing standards. The newsroom does not allow AI to alter photos, video, or audio, and it will not transmit AI-generated images that are false depictions, though such images may be used in a story if clearly labeled. Journalists are urged to verify external content for AI manipulation by checking sources, performing reverse image searches, and consulting trusted media reports.
